questions.prompt: By the CAP theorem, what must a distributed data store give up while a network partition is happening?
questions.answer: Either consistency or availability: refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer with possibly stale data to stay available
distractors: Partition tolerance, so that it can keep both consistency and availability
Durability: recent writes may be lost
Nothing, as long as there are at least three replicas
questions.explanation: Partitions happen whether you like it or not, so the real choice is C or A while one lasts. With no partition, a system can offer both.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
questions.answer: Horizontal adds more machines; vertical gives one machine more CPU or memory
distractors: Horizontal gives one machine more CPU or memory; vertical adds more machines
Horizontal scales the database; vertical scales the web tier
Horizontal is automatic; vertical is manual
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling is simple but has a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling needs stateless services (or partitioned state) and a load balancer.

questions.prompt: Which caching strategy has the application check the cache first and, on a miss, read from the database itself and put the result in the cache?
distractors: Write-through
Write-behind
Read-through
questions.explanation: In cache-aside the app owns the loading logic; with read-through the cache library loads from the database for you. Write-through and write-behind are about when writes reach the database.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an API operation to be idempotent?
questions.answer: Doing it several times has the same effect as doing it once, so a client can safely retry it
distractors: It always returns exactly the same response body
It has no side effects at all
The server only allows it to be called once
questions.explanation: DELETE /orders/7 twice leaves the order deleted either way, even if the second response is a 404. Idempotency is about the effect on the server, not identical responses; "no side effects" is the stronger property called safe.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is not idempotent by definition: GET, PUT, DELETE or POST?
distractors: PUT
DELETE
GET
questions.explanation: POST creates or triggers something each time, so retrying can create duplicates; APIs often add an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. PUT replaces a resource with the same state each time.

questions.prompt: Which resilience pattern stops calling a downstream service for a while after repeated failures, failing fast instead, then lets a trial request through to see whether it has recovered?
distractors: Retry with backoff
Bulkhead
Rate limiter
questions.explanation: Closed → open (fail fast) → half-open (one trial call). It protects both your threads and the struggling service; retries alone would add load to it.

questions.prompt: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff between retries?
questions.answer: So clients that failed at the same moment don't all retry in sync and swamp the recovering service again (a thundering herd)
distractors: To make each retry more likely to succeed on its own
To stop the retries from ever timing out
Because exact backoff intervals aren't allowed by HTTP
questions.explanation: Without jitter, a thousand clients that failed together retry together at 1 s, 2 s, 4 s... Randomising the delay spreads the load out.

questions.answer: Once writes stop, all replicas converge on the same value; until then, reads may return stale data
distractors: Every read returns the latest write, after a short delay
Data is written to disk eventually rather than immediately
Transactions are applied in a random order
questions.explanation: It's the availability-friendly choice: replicas accept reads and writes independently and sync in the background. Code has to tolerate briefly stale reads.

questions.prompt: Which technique spreads keys across cache or database nodes so that adding or removing a node only moves about 1/n of the keys?
distractors: Modulo hashing
Range partitioning
Round robin
questions.explanation: With `hash(key) % n`, changing n remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring, so a change only affects keys next to that node.

questions.prompt: Which load-balancing algorithm sends each new request to the server with the fewest active connections?
distractors: Round robin
IP hash
Random
questions.explanation: Least connections adapts when some requests are much slower than others. Round robin assumes every request costs the same; IP hash keeps a client on one server (sticky sessions).

questions.prompt: What is a message queue's dead-letter queue for?
questions.answer: Holding messages that couldn't be processed after several attempts (or expired), so they stop blocking the main queue and can be inspected
distractors: Storing messages whose consumer has shut down, until it restarts
Messages that should be deleted without being read
A backup copy of every message, for replay
questions.explanation: A "poison" message that always throws would otherwise be retried forever. Moving it aside keeps the queue flowing; alert on the DLQ and fix or replay its messages.

questions.prompt: With at-least-once message delivery, what property must consumers have so a redelivered message isn't processed twice?
distractors: Stateless
Single-threaded
Asynchronous
questions.explanation: Brokers redeliver when an acknowledgement is lost, so duplicates will happen. Record processed message ids, or make the operation naturally repeatable (an upsert rather than an increment).

questions.prompt: Which database technique copies data from a primary to read-only copies to spread out read traffic?
distractors: Sharding
Partitioning
Denormalisation
questions.explanation: Replicas scale reads (and give failover), but every write still goes to the primary, and asynchronous replicas can lag. Sharding splits the data itself, which also scales writes.

questions.answer: Splitting one dataset across several databases by a key (e.g. customer id), so each holds and serves part of the data
distractors: Keeping full copies of the database on several servers
Splitting a table's columns into separate tables
Encrypting each part of the database with a different key
questions.explanation: Sharding scales writes and storage. The costs are cross-shard queries and transactions, and hot shards if the key is badly chosen. Full copies are replication; splitting columns is vertical partitioning.
